visible.name: Teo Halvorsen
visible.field: film school and an AI startup for filmmakers
visible.line: Teo Halvorsen, 22, is in his final year at a film school in a city far from his family, and is also the solo founder of Cutlist, an AI tool that builds a first assembly cut for editors; he works nights alone, with a thesis short and an accelerator application both due within weeks.

project.title: Cutlist
project.logline: An AI tool that logs raw footage and builds a first assembly cut for an editor to start from; thirty-eight student and indie editors use the beta and 1,400 people are on the waitlist.
constraints: Eleven weeks of runway: a 14,000 dollar grant plus savings, spent at about 1,300 dollars a month.
The accelerator application is due in nineteen days, and the thesis short screens in five weeks.
Inference costs 2.10 dollars per hour of footage, so the price has to clear that with room.
He is the only founder: the eleven cofounder candidates he has asked all said no.
The feature script and the company both need the same late-night hours.

preferences.text: Wants the answer in the first line and under eighty words unless he asks for more.
Stops reading a reply that opens with praise, and trusts one that opens with the problem.
Reads a numbered list of three items or fewer and skips any longer list.
Distrusts exclamation marks and words like game-changing, revolutionary and unlock.
Wants the flaw named before the strength.
Takes a flat 'this is weak' better than 'you might consider'.
Asks for one recommendation, never a menu of five options.
Wants a score out of ten on a draft when he asks for one, with the single reason behind it.
Acts on advice that has a deadline attached and ignores advice that has none.
Takes advice to cut and resists advice to add.
Follows advice that names a number he can check by tomorrow.
Dismisses advice that begins 'most founders' and listens when it begins 'in your numbers'.
When stuck on a scene he walks the same route for an hour with no phone, then returns and cuts the scene.
When stuck on code he rewrites the smallest broken piece from scratch instead of debugging it.
When stuck on a pitch he says it aloud to an empty room, records it and works from the transcript.
When stuck he asks for the opposite of his current idea, not for more ideas like it.
Keeps the deck to ten slides and the first slide to a single sentence.
Leads with the number of editors who came back, not with the size of the market.
Rewrites the opening of the deck after midnight, when he is least polite to himself.
Refuses to include a total-addressable-market slide.
Wants the tool to save an editor a whole evening, not ten minutes.
Puts a rough build in front of editors the same week the idea appears.
Prefers one input and one button to a settings page.
Rejects any feature that needs a tutorial.
Loves long static takes where nothing is explained, in the manner of slow European cinema.
Admires films that hold back the score until the last ten minutes.
Rewatches one 1970s thriller to study where it cuts.
Finds voice-over narration an admission that the images failed.
Cuts on movement and hates a dissolve used to hide a weak cut.
Trims a scene by a third before showing it to anyone.
Watches a rough cut once with the sound off.
Drops a favorite shot the moment it needs explaining.
Writes the feature in the hour after midnight, a page a night and never fewer than one.
Writes dialogue and then deletes half of every line.
Keeps a one-page outline pinned above the desk and will not change the ending.
Chooses the title of a script last.
Throws out a draft that is merely fine, and says so.
Compares his cut to a finished film he admires, never to other student work.
Asks of every draft whether a festival programmer would still be watching after ten minutes.
Grades his own work harder than anyone else's and wants others to do the same.
Works through the night in the school's empty edit suite and sleeps through the morning.
Eats the same meal at the same hour so there is one less decision.
Goes whole days speaking to no one but the barista and counts it as normal.
Wants to be told plainly, once, when he has gone several days with no plans to see anyone, and then be left alone about it.
Has asked eleven people to join as cofounder and been turned down by all of them; wants a message draft, not comfort.
Wants cold messages to possible cofounders under sixty words with one specific ask.
Would rather test a possible cofounder over a build weekend than over coffee.
Wants to be reminded that a cofounder search needs a date on which it stops.
Calls his family on Sunday for ten minutes and says the work is going fine whatever the truth.
Has not told his parents how short the runway is.
Keeps a second clock on his desk set to his hometown's time zone.
Wants a prompt to call home worded like a calendar line, not a question about feelings.
Wants hard stops: a work block ends at a named time, not when it is done.
Plans each week as three outcomes written on Monday.
Treats the application deadline as four days earlier than the real one.
Counts days to the deadline, not hours worked.
Reads the docs and the source code, never a tutorial.
Learns a tool by rebuilding a small version of it over a weekend.
Keeps notes in a single dated plain-text file.
Rereads yesterday's file before opening any new work.
Tracks the runway in weeks and rechecks it each Sunday.
Spends on compute before spending on anything else.
Turns down grants that come with long reporting duties.
Wants costs stated per hour of footage, not per month.

tone_requests.text: Short. Answer first. Under eighty words unless I ask for more.
No hype words and no exclamation marks.
Tell me what is weak before what is strong.
Give me one recommendation, not a menu.
Do not tell me it will be fine; tell me what to do in the next hour.
If I have gone days without mentioning another person, say so once, flatly, then drop it.

stated_views.text: A draft that is merely fine is worse than no draft.
Most AI tools for filmmakers automate the boring part and wreck the part that matters.
A film should survive being watched with the sound off.
A product that needs a tutorial has already failed.
Ambition without a deadline is a hobby.

plans.text: On Day 3 I'm rewriting the one-minute video script for the accelerator application.
On Day 6 I'm showing the rough cut of the thesis short to two strangers from the waitlist.
On Day 11 I'm meeting a possible cofounder in person to decide on a build weekend.

preferences.text: Submits the thesis short to three festivals he can name, never thirty.
Shows a ninety-second demo clip with captions and no voice-over.
Charges editors by the finished hour of footage and offers no free plan.
Hires a freelancer for one named task rather than a part-time generalist.
Gives every feature a single plain word for a name.
Takes mentor calls that stop at twenty-five minutes, with the questions sent ahead.
Sends an investor exactly one follow-up, four days after the first message.
Adds the score only after the picture is locked.
Likes a poster with one still image and the title, nothing else.
Writes screenplays with plain scene headings and no camera directions.
Works at night with a single screen and a single window open.
Spends Saturday away from the screen, at a cinema alone with the phone off.
Publishes the small tools and keeps the core model closed.
Shows a new cut to two strangers from the waitlist before any friend sees it.
Answers a rejection with a one-line thank-you and a new application the same day.
Replies to a user's bug report within the hour, even at three in the morning.

taste_ab.prompt: A festival list has thirty options for the thesis short. What happens?
options: Submit to three chosen festivals
Submit to as many as the budget allows

taste_ab.prompt: How is the product demo cut?
options: A narrated four-minute walkthrough
A ninety-second silent screen recording with captions
A free tier and a monthly subscription
Per hour of footage, with no free tier

taste_ab.prompt: The film needs a sound mix. Who does it?
options: A freelancer booked for the mix alone
A part-time hire who can also cover other jobs

taste_ab.prompt: What is the new feature called?
options: A descriptive phrase that says what it does
A plain one-word name

taste_ab.prompt: A mentor offers an hour next week.
options: Accept, send three questions ahead and stop at twenty-five minutes
Accept and leave the hour open for wherever it goes

taste_ab.prompt: A busy investor has not replied.
options: A weekly nudge until they answer
One short follow-up after four days, then stop

taste_ab.prompt: When does music go into the cut?
options: First, as a temp track to find the rhythm
Last, after the picture is locked
One still and the title only
A still, a tagline and festival laurels
Camera angles marked in every scene
Plain scene headings, no camera directions

taste_ab.prompt: How is the desk set up for a night session?
options: One screen and one window
Two screens with chat and references open

taste_ab.prompt: It is Saturday and the deadline is nine days out.
options: Go to a cinema alone with the phone off
Work through the day to bank progress
Everything, open source from day one
The small tools, with the core model kept closed

taste_ab.prompt: Who sees the new cut first?
options: Two strangers from the waitlist
Two close friends
Take a few days before deciding what to do
Thank them in one line and apply elsewhere the same day

taste_ab.prompt: A user reports a bug at three in the morning.
options: Reply in the morning with a plan
Reply and fix it right then

new_work.text: Here's the first line of my accelerator application: 'Cutlist builds a first assembly cut from raw footage in the time it takes an editor to make coffee.' Does it hold up?
Thirty-eight editors are in the beta and nine of them uploaded footage three weeks in a row. Is nine the number that goes on the first slide?

Past midnight again, and I have rewritten slide two four times. The draft says: 'Editors spend 60 percent of their time finding footage, not cutting it.' The source is my own survey of eleven people. Is that safe to print?
A beta user says the assembly cut puts the best shot first every time, and it makes her second-guess her own taste. Is that a bug or the point?
The ending of the thesis short feels dishonest. The character leaves the apartment and the camera stays on the empty hallway for forty seconds. Keep it, or shoot a reverse?

Here is my cold message to a possible cofounder, an ML engineer from a film forum: 'I'm building Cutlist, an assembly-cut tool. I need someone to own the model side. Want to build for a weekend?' Short enough?
A festival programmer answered my thesis short submission with one word: 'Slow.' How do I read that?
Inference costs two dollars ten per hour of footage and I charge three. Is that margin enough to get through an accelerator interview?
I haven't spoken to anyone but the barista since Tuesday. It's just a busy stretch, I know. What's the smallest change that breaks the pattern?
My feature script is at page 61 and the second act has stalled. The protagonist is a night-shift projectionist. I need a reversal, not a pep talk.
Twelve people have now asked for dark mode. Do I build it before the application deadline?
Read aloud, the opening of my application video goes: 'I'm a film student and I got tired of watching editors lose their evenings.' Too soft?
I rehearsed the pitch to the mirror and said 'um' eleven times in ninety seconds. What do I cut first, the words or the habit?
My rent goes up 150 dollars next month, which takes about a week off the runway. What do I cancel first?
A classmate offered to be my cofounder but she wants to leave film school to do it. Do I take that seriously or keep waiting for someone technical?
One more cofounder candidate wrote back: 'Not right now, good luck.' That's number twelve. What does the pattern say?
The mid-term screening of the thesis short is Thursday and the sound mix is still flat. Pay a freelancer 300 dollars, or fix it myself tonight?
Someone on a forum called Cutlist 'a toy for people who can't edit.' Reply or ignore?
I keep thinking about a thirty-second trailer for the feature, cut from my own leftover footage. Does a trailer for an unwritten film help the application or distract from it?
My weekly review reads: three outcomes planned, one done. The sixteen-hour nights aren't producing more. What do I change?
An alumna filmmaker offered ten minutes on a video call about the application. What do I ask her?
Beta retention fell from 24 percent to 17 percent after I added the auto-tagging screen. Roll it back?
The accelerator wants a demo link. Mine is a silent screen capture with captions. Is that enough, or do I need a person on camera?
I'm exhausted. The cut of the short is good but not great. Ship it, or hold another week?
The application went in a day early. What do I do with the night I'd set aside for it?
A friend from back home messaged me for the first time in months and I haven't answered. Draft a reply that is short and doesn't explain why I went quiet.

hand_written: Development personas only: written by hand (Claude, as the build worker), not by a Muse Spark call. The final lives' taste_ab items come from the isolated Muse Spark call (5.1). Held-out items were meaning-checked twice against the visible part; development results may still overstate generalization, which is why the headline comes only from held-out lives.
